subject: ela
description: Students determine an author's point of view or purpose in an informational text and explain how that point of view or purpose is conveyed through the text. They distinguish purpose (the reason the author wrote the piece, such as to inform, to explain, to persuade, to warn, to describe, or to call the reader to act) from point of view (the author's attitude, stance, or position toward the topic). They identify whether the author is neutral or takes a side, and which side. They then point to specific evidence in the text that conveys that purpose or stance, including word choice and loaded language, tone, the selection and emphasis of details, direct statements of opinion, the way counterarguments are handled, and the use of questions, examples, or appeals to the reader. They explain how those textual choices work together to reveal the author's purpose or point of view. Every item embeds the full passage or excerpt it depends on, so the student needs nothing external. There is no math.
subSkills: Determine the author's purpose in a text (to inform, explain, describe, persuade, warn, entertain, or call the reader to act) and state it in the student's own words
Determine the author's point of view, attitude, or stance toward the topic (neutral, positive, negative, concerned, admiring, critical) and identify which side the author takes
Distinguish purpose (why the author wrote it) from point of view (how the author feels about the topic) and from the topic itself
Identify word choice and loaded or connotative language that signals the author's stance or feeling toward the subject
Use tone (the author's attitude as expressed through language) as evidence of point of view
Recognize how the selection, emphasis, or omission of details reveals what the author wants the reader to think or feel
Locate direct statements of opinion or position and separate them from neutral statements of fact
Explain how specific textual choices work together to convey the author's purpose or point of view, citing evidence from the passage
Notice how an author handles other viewpoints or counterarguments and what that reveals about the author's own stance

problemArchetypes.name: Determine the author's purpose
problemArchetypes.example: Read the short passage. What is the author's main purpose in writing this text? Answer: The author's purpose is to persuade readers that cities should build more bike lanes, shown by the repeated arguments in favor and the call for readers to support the plan.

problemArchetypes.name: Determine the author's point of view or stance
problemArchetypes.example: Read the paragraph. What is the author's point of view about year-round school? Answer: The author is opposed to it, treating it as a burden on families rather than describing it neutrally.

problemArchetypes.name: Identify the evidence that conveys purpose or point of view
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. Which detail most clearly shows the author's attitude toward fast fashion? Answer: The phrase describing it as a wasteful habit that fills landfills reveals a critical, disapproving stance.

problemArchetypes.name: Analyze word choice and loaded language as a signal of stance
problemArchetypes.example: Read the sentence in context. How does the word choice reveal the author's point of view? Answer: Calling the policy a reckless gamble rather than a plan shows the author disapproves of it, because reckless and gamble carry negative feelings.

problemArchetypes.name: Distinguish purpose from point of view from topic
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. The topic is electric cars. What is the difference between the author's purpose and the author's point of view here? Answer: The purpose is to convince readers to consider electric cars, while the point of view is that electric cars are a smart and responsible choice.

problemArchetypes.name: Explain how a structural or rhetorical choice conveys purpose or stance
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. How does the author's choice to open with a question and end with a warning convey the purpose? Answer: The opening question pulls the reader in and the closing warning pushes the reader to act, working together to persuade rather than simply inform.

problemArchetypes.name: Analyze how the author treats an opposing view
problemArchetypes.example: Read the passage. How does the way the author mentions the opposing argument reveal the author's own point of view? Answer: The author states the opposing view only to dismiss it quickly as outdated, which shows the author firmly supports the other side.

Easy.description: A short stimulus (one or two paragraphs, roughly 40 to 90 words) embedded in the item, with a clearly stated or strongly signaled purpose or stance. The task is to identify the author's purpose, identify the author's point of view, or pick the single detail that most obviously shows it. The stance is overt, often marked by clear opinion words or obvious loaded language, so little inference is required.
constraints: Stimulus is one or two short paragraphs of roughly 40 to 90 words included in the prompt
Tests one concept: name the purpose, name the point of view, or pick the most obvious supporting detail
Identify-level task in which the stance is openly stated or marked by clear opinion words such as should, must, best, or worst
Minimal inference; the author's attitude is on the surface and not hidden or mixed

Medium.description: A moderate stimulus (a multi-paragraph section, roughly 100 to 180 words) embedded in the item, in which the purpose or point of view is present but conveyed through word choice, tone, and the selection of details rather than stated outright. The task requires analysis: explaining how specific language or details convey the stance, distinguishing purpose from point of view, or determining a stance that is implied rather than declared. The student must reason from textual evidence to the author's attitude.
constraints: Stimulus is a multi-paragraph section of roughly 100 to 180 words in the prompt
Tests how word choice, tone, or detail selection conveys the purpose or point of view, with the stance implied rather than stated
Analyze-level task: connect specific evidence in the passage to the author's purpose or attitude
Distractors are plausible and confuse purpose with point of view, mistake the topic for the stance, or name an attitude the text does not support

Hard.description: A complex stimulus (a complete short informational text or a passage that weighs more than one viewpoint, roughly 190 to 280 words) embedded in the item. The purpose or point of view is conveyed subtly, through tone, the handling of counterarguments, what is emphasized or left out, and accumulated word choice. The task requires evaluation: explaining how several textual choices work together to convey the stance, judging how the author's treatment of an opposing view reveals point of view, or comparing the author's stated purpose with the attitude that shows through the language. Requires inference about authorial intent and the combined effect of multiple choices.
constraints: Stimulus is a complete short informational text or a multi-viewpoint passage of roughly 190 to 280 words in the prompt
Tests how multiple choices (tone, loaded language, detail selection, handling of counterarguments) work together to convey purpose or point of view
Evaluate-level task: explain the combined effect of the author's choices or how the treatment of an opposing view reveals the author's stance
Requires inference about authorial intent; distractors reflect partial readings, surface tone, or confusing a balanced presentation with neutrality

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses the author's point of view with the topic or subject of the text
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Answers that the author's point of view is simply the subject, such as saying the point of view is recycling, instead of stating the author's attitude toward recycling

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student confuses purpose (why the author wrote the text) with point of view (how the author feels about the topic)
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Names the author's purpose, such as to inform, when asked for the point of view, or names a stance when asked for the purpose

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student assumes any informational text is automatically neutral and overlooks a clear persuasive stance
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Claims the author is balanced or has no opinion even when loaded language and one-sided detail selection show the author clearly favors one side

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student selects a true detail from the passage that does not actually reveal the author's purpose or stance
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Points to a neutral fact stated in the text as the evidence of the author's attitude, when that fact carries no opinion or feeling

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student substitutes the student's own opinion about the topic for the author's point of view
commonMisconceptions.distractor: States what the student personally believes about the subject rather than the attitude the author expresses in the text

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student ignores word choice and tone and judges the stance only by the topic or the first sentence
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Misses loaded or connotative words like reckless, wonderful, or dangerous and so assigns a stance opposite to the one the language conveys

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student treats the author's mention of an opposing view as the author's own position
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Adopts a counterargument that the author raises only to dismiss, reporting it as the author's point of view

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Student names an attitude or purpose that is stronger or different from what the text supports
commonMisconceptions.distractor: Overstates a mildly concerned author as outraged, or labels an informative passage as persuasive when no argument or call to act is present
